source.title_on_document: Effects of AI-generated images in visual art education on students' classroom engagement, self-efficacy and cognitive load

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or online appendix is mentioned in the full 14-page PDF, and none is included; absence of a reference does not establish that none exists elsewhere. The reported outcome statistics are in the main text (p. 11, Table 9). Data availability (p. 12) states: "No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study." No data or code repository is named.

paper_design_summary: The study analyzed 78 fifth graders from two classes at a primary school in Shandong Province, China, with 39 students per group; the abstract says assignment was random, but the introduction calls the study quasi-experimental and the allocation procedure is not described (pp. 1, 2, 4; p. 11, Table 9). For Task 2, the same teacher illustrated the lesson with AI-generated cartoon images for the treatment group and classical cartoon artworks for the control group; the described procedure has a research assistant supply the AI images and students paint by hand (p. 6, Stage 3; p. 12, fourth limitation). Three teachers rated each painting on five rubric criteria, including creativity and originality, while separate questionnaires measured engagement, self-efficacy, and cognitive load (p. 6, Stage 4; pp. 8-11, Results).

studies.label: Classroom experiment: AI-generated vs classical example images in a fifth-grade cartoon-painting lesson

assignment.what_was_assigned: The source of the example images in the teacher's Task 2 slides: AI-generated artwork (treatment) versus classical cartoon artworks (control; p. 6, Stage 3). The abstract reports random assignment of 78 students, 39 per group (p. 1), but the introduction calls the study quasi-experimental (p. 2), the Methods and Discussion say only assigned (pp. 4, 9), and the consent statement calls it a non-interventional questionnaire-based study (p. 14). The actual allocation unit and method are unresolved. randomized = not_stated is the form's available uncertainty code for this conflicting report, not a claim that the abstract omits random assignment. design_class = other avoids asserting either a verified RCT or verified non-random assignment.
assignment.quote: Seventy-eight fifth-grade students were randomly assigned to a treatment group (n = 39) and a control group (n = 39).
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract (randomly assigned); p. 2, Introduction (quasi-experimental); p. 4, Methods, Participants; p. 9, Discussion, opening paragraph; p. 14, Informed consent. Fig. 2 (p. 5) shows treatment and control groups but no allocation procedure or class-to-arm mapping. The randomized artworks in Stage 4 (p. 6) concern presentation to raters, not treatment allocation. The two classes and two arms each contain 39 students; those counts do not distinguish individual allocation from intact-class allocation. unit = other records the unknown allocation unit.

arms.name: Treatment (GAI-assisted teaching)
arms.description: Task 2 taught with the GAI-assisted method: the teacher's PowerPoint instruction used anthropomorphic cartoon images that a research assistant generated with Stable Diffusion (Fig. 3), followed by hand painting with sketching pencils, watercolor paints, and art paper. Fig. 2 also lists interviews for this group only, at Stage 4 after the paintings; no interview results are reported.

arms.name: Control (conventional teaching)
arms.description: Task 2 taught by the same teacher with the same lesson structure, using classical artworks of iconic cartoon characters (Fig. 4), followed by hand painting with the same tools.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The abstract reports 78 students assigned, 39 per group (p. 1); Tables 1, 3 to 7, and 9 print n = 39 per group (pp. 4, 8, 9, 11). The analyzed sample is 78 people. n_randomized is null for the study and arms because randomization is unresolved, not because the reported assignment counts are missing.
participants.who: Fifth-grade primary school students aged 10 to 12 (mean 11.13, SD 0.437), 41 male and 37 female, from two classes (Class A and Class B, 39 students each).
participants.country: China (Shandong Province). The Methods do not name the school. Three authors list Qingdao Ningxia Road Primary School, Qingdao, as their affiliation (p. 1).
participants.quote: This study involved 78 fifth-grade students from a primary school in Shandong Province, China. The participants were drawn from two classes: Class A (39 students) and Class B (39 students), comprising 41 males and 37 females.
participants.locator: p. 4, Methods, Participants; p. 4, Table 1; p. 1, Abstract; p. 11, Table 9 (n = 39 per group)

ai_tool.name_model: Stable Diffusion (checkpoints named in Fig. 3: realvisxlV40_v40LightningBakedvae, AnythingXL_xl, cartoonArcadiaSDXLSD1_xenoArcadiaCX)
ai_tool.how_used: The teacher used AI-generated cartoon images as examples in the Task 2 PowerPoint instruction; both groups painted with traditional tools (p. 6, Stage 3; p. 7, Fig. 3). The fourth limitation says "a research assistant obtained the AI-generated images for them" (p. 12), supporting ideas_supplied without student operation of the generator. The Discussion nevertheless describes involving students in image generation (p. 9, Firstly) and rapid prototyping before traditional refinement (p. 11, Fourthly); no such student procedure is described in the Methods. These conflicting Discussion claims are not used to infer direct AI use. Whether the supplied images remained available during painting practice is not stated.

task.description: Task 2, "Anthropomorphic Cartoon Character": "Using the anthropomorphism techniques you have learned, create and design a distinct and characteristic anthropomorphic cartoon character", painted with sketching pencils, watercolor paints, and standard art paper (p. 6).
task.duration: Stage 3 (teacher instruction plus painting practice) lasted approximately 40 minutes (p. 6). The Participants section describes the cartoon-painting module as two 20-minute sessions (p. 4). The paper does not say how these sessions map onto Stages 1 to 4.

outcomes.name: Creativity and Originality (rubric score of the Task 2 painting)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric item "Creativity and Originality: How unique and imaginative is the artwork?" scored 1 to 5 by three teachers, two art teachers and one math teacher (rubric p. 6; raters p. 10, Table 8). Rater Z is also the instructor of the experiment (p. 8), although p. 6 says raters were blinded to group and the artworks were anonymized and randomized. ICC for the composite score averaged across all rubric criteria = 0.847, p < 0.001 (p. 9); no item-level ICC is reported. How the three raters' scores are combined per painting is not stated. The item could also be read as novelty ("unique"). AI-image availability during painting is not stated: Stage 3 contains teacher instruction and student painting practice, but does not say whether the examples remained accessible (p. 6). ai_available_when_produced is null; with_ai is retained provisionally for the lesson using supplied AI examples. If the examples were removed before painting, the question would need review for after_ai under codebook sections 1 and 6; a separate later session is not required.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear because the abstract states random assignment (p. 1), the introduction calls the design quasi-experimental (p. 2), and neither the allocation unit nor procedure is described in the Methods or flow diagram (pp. 4-5). The equal class and arm sizes do not distinguish individual from class allocation. Class allocation would not by itself establish non-random assignment; the actual method must be confirmed. design_class is other and context_class remains none pending clarification, rather than asserting an RCT or non-randomized observational context. The AI contrast itself is in scope: supplied AI-generated example images versus human-made examples are ideas_supplied and ai_vs_active under codebook sections 5-6 (p. 6, Stage 3; p. 12, fourth limitation). Direct student operation of the generator is not required. Criterion 2 is met by 78 people analyzed, 39 per group (p. 4, Participants; p. 11, Table 9). Criterion 3 is met by teachers scoring each student's painting on Creativity and Originality (p. 6, Stage 4; p. 11, Table 9). Unreported availability of the example images during painting affects with_ai versus after_ai classification, not these two confirmed eligibility criteria or the existence of AI exposure.

one_line_finding: Fifth graders taught with Stable Diffusion example images received higher teacher ratings for Creativity and Originality of their hand-painted cartoon characters than those taught with classical cartoon artworks (4.581, SD 0.444, vs 4.205, SD 0.499, n = 39 each; t = 3.515, p < 0.001), and higher ratings on the other four rubric criteria (p. 11, Table 9).
open_questions: What were the allocation unit and procedure, and was allocation random? The abstract says randomly assigned (p. 1), the introduction says quasi-experimental (p. 2), and the Methods and flow diagram provide no randomization method or class-to-arm mapping (pp. 4-5). Equal class and arm sizes do not resolve the question. This also leaves the historical reconciliation differences over design_class and context_class unresolved.

Were the AI-generated example images still visible or otherwise accessible during painting, or had they been removed? Stage 3 separates instruction and painting practice without stating access during practice (p. 6). Availability is null and with_ai is provisional; removal could require after_ai even within the same session.

How was rater blinding implemented for Rater Z, who was also the instructor (p. 8)? Stage 4 reports anonymized, randomized artworks and blinded raters (p. 6); the instructor role creates a masking concern but does not prove that masking failed.

Were the Table 9 tests one-sided or two-sided, and what testing convention produced the printed p-values (p. 11)? The paper does not state sidedness. All t and p values are retained exactly as printed, without replacing them with calculated values.

How were the three teachers' scores combined into each student's Table 9 score? The paper reports participant counts and an ICC for a composite across rubric criteria, but does not state the aggregation rule across raters (p. 6, Stage 4; p. 9, ICC; p. 11, Table 9).

How do the two 20-minute sessions in Methods, Participants (p. 4) map onto the research stages, whose instruction-and-painting stages are each described as approximately 40 minutes (pp. 5-6)? Both duration statements are retained without inferring a schedule.
notes: Only outcomes scored on the paintings are listed: the five rubric criteria in Table 9 (p. 11). Self-reported classroom engagement (Tables 3-4), self-efficacy (Tables 5-6), and cognitive load (Table 7) are not qualifying output outcomes. Fig. 2 (p. 5) lists Task 1 painting ratings at the Stage 2 pretest and treatment-group interviews at Stage 4, but neither result is reported. The Data analysis section says t-tests and ANCOVA were performed on painting scores (p. 6), but only t-tests are reported (p. 11, Table 9). Table 9 prints n = 39 per group for each rubric criterion; Stage 3 assigns one character painting to each student and Stage 4 evaluates all participants' paintings (p. 6). unit is participant and n_units remains null. The exact aggregation across raters is not stated. All printed arm counts, means, SDs, t statistics, and p-values in Table 9 were checked against the PDF text. No effect size, degrees of freedom, alternate p-value, or standard error is calculated or substituted. Test sidedness remains an author question. Inconsistencies in the paper: Stage 4 calls the raters "Three professional visual art teachers" (p. 6), but Table 8 lists one math teacher (p. 10). The Discussion says treatment students "expressed high levels of satisfaction with their visual artworks" (p. 11), whereas Table 9 and the Methods describe teacher ratings. The fourth limitation names ChatGPT (p. 12), whereas the Methods and Fig. 3 identify Stable Diffusion (pp. 4, 7). The informed-consent statement calls the work "a non-interventional questionnaire-based study" (p. 14), conflicting with the classroom intervention described in the Methods. The Results text reports affective-engagement F = 17.279 (p. 8), whereas Table 4 prints 17.379 (p. 9); this is a self-report outcome not coded here. Table 9 prints the row label "Creativity and Originalit". The Discussion describes student participation in image generation (p. 9, Firstly) and says "GAI enables rapid prototyping allowing students to experiment freely with diverse techniques before refining outputs through traditional methods" (p. 11, Fourthly). The actual procedure describes teacher slides and traditional painting tools (p. 6), and the fourth limitation says a research assistant obtained the images because teachers and students could not independently generate them (p. 12). The supply-of-examples coding follows the procedure; the Discussion claims do not establish direct student AI use or continuing image access during painting. The country is China; the Methods identify only a primary school in Shandong Province (p. 4), not the Qingdao school named in author affiliations (p. 1). Final coding uses other for unresolved design and not_stated for unresolved randomization; these reflect contradictory reporting rather than confirmed non-random assignment. n_randomized is null, while the abstract's reported assignment counts remain documented and analyzed counts remain 78 total and 39 per arm. Availability is null because the schema has no uncertainty category for that field; mixed would incorrectly assert known variation. with_ai is provisional. Supplied AI examples qualify under the codebook without direct generator operation. Technical Skill and Composition and Design retain usefulness because the current codebook explicitly includes output quality; the separate Creativity and Originality score establishes criterion 3. The full markdown, including references and end matter, and relevant PDF pages were read; Fig. 2, Fig. 3 model names, and the publication date were also checked in PDF renders held in memory. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical screening provenance. Final decisions supersede its provisional design, randomization, counts, and availability statements; challenge counts describe form corrections, while unresolved factual questions remain in final.open_items.

open_items.item: Randomization and allocation unit: the original assignment open question and both unresolved reconciliation differences (studies[S1].design_class and eligibility.context_class) require the actual allocation protocol, unit, and method from the authors. The protocol must reconcile the abstract's random assignment with the quasi-experimental label and establish whether people or classes were assigned, and how. This determines criterion 1 and RCT versus non-randomized context classification; equal counts settle neither.

Original question about whether supplied AI images count as assistance is settled by codebook section 6: ideas_supplied includes AI-generated ideas or examples. The documented image intervention (p. 6, Stage 3; p. 12, fourth limitation) fits without students operating the generator. No further criterion 1 scope decision is needed on direct tool use.

AI-image access during painting: authors must say whether the images remained projected or otherwise available during student practice, or were removed after instruction (p. 6, Stage 3). This settles provisional with_ai versus possible after_ai coding; both questions are in scope, so it does not independently change eligibility.

Rater blinding: authors must explain how artwork masking worked for Rater Z, the instructor, and whether that rater could identify the groups (p. 6, Stage 4; p. 8, Results). This concerns risk of rating bias, not whether creativity was scored on participant output.

Table 9 test sidedness: authors must identify the one-sided or two-sided convention and clarify the reported t/p combinations (p. 11). Printed statistics are preserved; this affects statistical interpretation, not any eligibility criterion.

Aggregation across raters: authors must provide the scoring rule used to combine the three teachers' ratings into each student's Table 9 outcome (p. 6, Stage 4; p. 9, ICC; p. 11, Table 9). The reported 78 analyzed people and direct creativity scoring already establish criteria 2 and 3.

Duration mapping retained in reconciliation.differences for task.duration: authors must reconcile the two 20-minute sessions (p. 4, Participants) with the approximately 40-minute instruction-and-painting stages (pp. 5-6). The reconciliation retained both printed statements but did not establish their mapping. This affects intervention description, not an eligibility criterion.
